parts.label: (a)(i)
key_concepts: frequency as oscillations per unit time
hints: Hint 1: Think about what one single oscillation of the loudspeaker creates in the air - how far does that one wavefront travel forward before the next one starts?
Hint 2: Think about the definition linking number of oscillations N, frequency f and time t, then rearrange it to make t the subject.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Distance for N waves**
Each oscillation of the loudspeaker sends out one complete wavelength into the air. So one oscillation means the wave has advanced by $\lambda$. For $N$ oscillations in a row, the first wavefront has kept moving while the others are produced behind it. The total distance covered is $N$ times one wavelength. That gives $$\text{distance} = N\lambda$$

Step 2: **Time for N oscillations**
Frequency tells you oscillations per second, so $$f = N/t$$ This is just number counted divided by time taken. Rearranging to make time the subject gives $$t = N/f$$ You now have both distance and time written only with $N$, $\lambda$ and $f$.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Remember speed is always distance divided by time, so try putting your two expressions from (i) together in that form and see what cancels.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Combine distance and time**
Speed is distance travelled divided by time taken. Using your results: $$v = \frac{\text{distance}}{\text{time}} = \frac{N\lambda}{N/f}$$ The $N$ on top and bottom cancel, leaving $$v = f\lambda$$ This is the famous wave equation. It shows one wavelength $\lambda$ passes per period, $f$ times per second.

parts.label: (b)
hints: Hint 1: Look along the horizontal time axis in Fig. 5.1 and count how many cm wide one complete cycle is, then think what the 0.20 ms per cm setting means for that width.
Hint 2: Once you have the period T in seconds, recall how period and frequency are linked by a reciprocal relationship.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find the period from the trace**
On the CRO the horizontal direction is time. One full sine wave stretches over 4.0 cm. Each cm represents 0.20 ms, so $$T = 4.0 \times 0.20\text{ ms} = 0.80\text{ ms} = 8.0 \times 10^{-4}\text{ s}$$ A common slip is to count peak to peak incorrectly or to forget to convert ms to s.

Step 2: **Convert period to frequency**
Frequency is the reciprocal of period: $$f = \frac{1}{T} = \frac{1}{8.0 \times 10^{-4}} = 1250\text{ Hz}$$ To 2 significant figures this is $$f \approx 1.3 \times 10^{3}\text{ Hz}$$

parts.label: (c)(i)
hints: Hint 1: For a stable interference pattern of loud and quiet points, the way the two sources line up with each other must not drift randomly with time.
parts.proper_answer: Coherent waves have a constant phase difference between them.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Meaning of coherent**
Two sources are coherent when they vibrate with the same frequency and their relative timing never changes. In wave language that is a constant phase difference. Because the phase difference stays fixed, the positions where waves add constructively and where they cancel destructively stay fixed in space, so you hear steady L and Q points.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: At a minimum of loudness the two sound displacements must be pulling the air in opposite directions at every instant, so picture how many degrees out of step that is.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Condition for a quiet point**
Minimum loudness Q is destructive interference. The crest of one wave always arrives with the trough of the other, so they cancel. That happens when the waves are exactly half a cycle out of step, which is a phase difference of $$180^{\circ}$$ Any odd multiple such as $540^{\circ}$ is physically the same condition, but the smallest is $180^{\circ}$.

parts.label: (c)(iii)
hints: Hint 1: Start at X where the two paths are equal, then follow the detector to Y and count how many loud maxima L are passed to work out how many extra wavelengths of path difference have built up.
Hint 2: Use the given $S_{2}Y = 7.40\text{ m}$ and wavelength $0.85\text{ m}$ to turn that path difference into an actual value for $S_{1}Y$.
parts.proper_answer: Path difference at Y is $2\lambda$, so $S_{1}Y = 7.40 + 2 \times 0.85 = 9.1\text{ m}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Count the path difference at Y**
At X, $S_{1}X = S_{2}X$ so path difference is zero and you get a maximum L. Moving toward Y you meet Q, L, Q, L. Each step from L to next L adds one whole $\lambda$ to the path difference. From X (0) to the final L at Y you have passed two intervals, so $$S_{1}Y - S_{2}Y = 2\lambda$$ This is constructive interference of second order.

Step 2: **Calculate $S_{1}Y$**
With $\lambda = 0.85\text{ m}$ and $S_{2}Y = 7.40\text{ m}$: $$S_{1}Y = S_{2}Y + 2\lambda = 7.40 + 2 \times 0.85$$ $$S_{1}Y = 7.40 + 1.70 = 9.10\text{ m} \approx 9.1\text{ m}$$ The $S_{1}$ path is longer because Y is further from $S_{1}$ than from $S_{2}$.
